title: Phase 0's prior cannot be written before the first search when the topic itself arrives by search — and the search that finds the topic contaminates the prior it is supposed to precede
expected: A prior written from the researcher's own standing model of the world, uncontaminated by retrieved material, so that the Phase 6 discovery/mirror call is a real test.
got: Phase 0 says 'before the first search, write down what you already think is going on'. My seat's topic is 'whatever broke this morning' — I ran a topic-discovery search FIRST, read a synthesised summary of the event, and only then wrote the prior. The prior I wrote ('escalation management dressed as routine enforcement') is measurably downstream of that summary's framing. The prompt has no slot for a retrieval act that precedes the prior, so the run either breaks the ordering rule or pretends search 0 was not a search.
note: Not lens. This bites any run where the topic is discovered rather than assigned — a breach found in a feed, a filing found in a docket sweep, a delisting found on a wire. The fix is one paragraph: split Phase 0 into a standing prior (before any retrieval) and a first-contact prior (written from the headline alone, before Phase 1), and make the discovery/mirror call against the standing one. Both already fit the existing field with a second key.

title: `search_scope` specifies the registers SEARCHED and has no field for the registers NOT searched — so every absence card is a completeness claim with no way to state its own incompleteness
expected: An absence card that a reviewer can tell apart from a laundered gap: what was searched, what was NOT, and therefore whether this is an absence in the world or an absence in the researcher's reach.
got: NOTEBOOK-SCHEMA.md:76 specifies `search_scope` as '(the register searched, the period, the request reference)'. Three of my four absence cards were absences in MY REACH, not in the world — I never opened the Federal Register, never searched Persian-language media, never searched the naval-law journals. A card listing three registers searched renders identically to one listing thirty. I had to invent a `not_searched` array to make the cards honest, and I only invented it because I was being watched for exactly this failure. Without it, `kind: "absence"` is a strictly better-looking home for a gap than `research_gaps` is, which inverts the incentive the field was created to fix.
note: This is the orchestrator's second hypothesis answered in the direction they feared, with the mechanism named. `kind: "absence"` is NOT unusable — it is the most useful new field in the schema. The hazard is that it is more prestigious than `research_gaps` and cheaper to satisfy, and the schema gives the reader no instrument to tell a four-register absence from a thirty-register one. Fix: make `search_scope` a required object of {searched[], not_searched[], period, what_would_count, as_of}, and make `not_searched` non-optional. An absence whose author cannot say where they did not look has not established an absence.

An adjacent counter-case is the MOST common shape on a fresh topic and currently the only one with no name.

title: A `derived` fact's source is arithmetic and `evidence_class` has no value for it, so three of mine are classed `primary` — the most flattering available answer
expected: A derived fact states the class of its own derivation, distinctly from the class of its inputs.

My three derived facts are computed by me from other facts in the same notebook. I wrote `{ name: "computed from f-tally-aug11", evidence_class: "primary", locator: "this notebook, method field" }`. The method IS inspectable, so `primary` is arguable — but it is arguable in exactly the direction that makes the notebook look better, and a class that flatters by default is the shape the whole `evidence_class` edit was written against. A derived fact should inherit the WEAKEST class among its `derived_from` inputs, not assert a class of its own.
note: Self-reported stuff. I filled this field wrong in the flattering direction and I am reporting it because the orchestrator asked which fields I stuffed. Fix: `evidence_class: "derived"` as a seventh value, defined as 'the weakest class among derived_from, plus a published method'. My f-derived-intervals would then be `vendor`, which is what it actually is — both its input dates come from one maritime-risk vendor — and that would show on the card instead of hiding behind exact subtraction.
